title: Impact of extraction methods on the properties of Carica papaya pseudostem fibers from Cameroon used as reinforcement in

predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The text states: 'Cameroon ranks 64th in the world in papaya production, with an annual output of 44 tons, which generates a large mass of Carica papaya (CP) trunk at the end of production.' An annual national output of only 44 tons is implausibly small for a country ranked 64th in global papaya production (global papaya production is in the millions of tons, and even minor producing countries typically report thousands of tons annually). This figure is almost certainly off by several orders of magnitude (likely missing a 'thousand' or similar unit), making the statistic internally implausible and inconsistent with the claim that it 'generates a large mass' of waste trunk.

Section 2.2 states that after water retting, 'the fibers could be extracted before being rinsed and sun-dried for 24 h to remove moisture.' However, Section 2.3 states 'The fibers extracted by the different techniques were dried at 28 °C in the sun for 72 h to reduce the water content. These were fibers extracted by water retting and fibers extracted chemically...' This directly contradicts the earlier stated 24 h drying time for the same water-retted fiber batch, giving two different drying durations (24 h vs 72 h) for the identical process step.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section describing FTIR and TGA sample preparation
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Both the FTIR method ('Samples of a few milligrams of powder (0.3 μm) were scanned...') and the TGA method ('Approximately 20 mg of extracted fiber powder, ground to a size of 0.3 μm, was heated...') describe grinding fiber powder down to 0.3 micrometers. Achieving sub-micron (0.3 μm) particle size via manual/standard laboratory grinding of plant fibers is essentially impossible without specialized nano-milling equipment, which is not described; this value is physically implausible and likely should be in millimeters, indicating a methodological description error repeated in two places.

The text defines water absorption degree W(%) in equation (2) as (Mf/Mi - 1) x 100, specific to water-saturated vs anhydrous fiber mass. Later, for the separate relative humidity recovery test (different conditioning procedure, different physical quantity 'a'), the text states 'the relative humidity, a, was calculated using relation 2,' reusing the water absorption equation without presenting or justifying a distinct formula appropriate for humidity recovery, creating ambiguity/inconsistency between two conceptually distinct measurements sharing one equation reference.

The abstract states: 'In contrast to the decrease in diameter, the measured density of Carica papaya pseudostem fibers increased with NaOH concentration,' implying a monotonic trend with increasing NaOH%. However, the body text reports diameters of 196.33 ± 4 μm (2.5% NaOH), 221.94 ± 6 μm (5% NaOH), and 219.31 ± 4 μm (7.5% NaOH) — a non-monotonic pattern (diameter increases from 2.5% to 5% NaOH before slightly decreasing at 7.5%), which does not support a claim of continuous diameter decrease with increasing NaOH concentration.

The abstract concludes 'Carica papaya fiber extracted at a concentration of 2.5 % will be the most suitable for biocomposite applications,' yet the same abstract reports that thermal stability at 2.5% NaOH (215 °C) is lower than that of the untreated water-retted fiber (220 °C), and explicitly states 'The tensile properties of these fibers showed great variability, and an influence of diameter was observed, indicating the need to study the influence of technique and NaOH mass concentration.' Drawing a definitive 'most suitable' conclusion despite acknowledged high variability and inferior thermal stability relative to the water-retted baseline overstates what the reported evidence supports.

The text states fiber samples (natural fibers of ~200 μm diameter) were 'subjected to a load of 5 kN at a loading speed of 5 mm min⁻¹.' Given the reported tensile strengths (~287 MPa) and small fiber cross-sectional areas, the force required to break such fibers is on the order of a few Newtons, not kilonewtons; describing the test as subjecting samples to a 5 kN load (rather than specifying the testing machine's load-cell capacity) is physically implausible for single natural fiber tensile testing as described.
